question: Is it halal to eat the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab sold in Western marketplaces?
answer:
This is going to be a long lecture with detailed evidences. So if you don't have time to listen to the entire lecture, with the evidences and with all of the madhhabs, I'm going to start off by summarizing my conclusion in two minutes, and then inshallah those that are able to can listen to the entire lecture.

**The position that I follow is that it is not allowed to eat non-zabihah meat, for three reasons**, in order of the strength of those reasons.

First and foremost, because a majority of scholars place the condition that Allah's name must be mentioned at the time of slaughter, and the meat that is available in the common marketplaces does not mention the name of Allah. And the majority position, which I will defend, is that this applies to both the Muslim and the Kitabi, or the Ahl al-Kitab.

Secondly, the presumption that the slaughterer is a person from the Ahl al-Kitab, from the Jewish or Christian background, is a presumption that is not certain, given the rising trend of agnosticism and atheism. It is difficult to categorically declare that modern societies (especially European societies more than America; Canadian and European more than American; but overall in the Western world) are all Ahl al-Kitab. To just simply assume that they are all Ahl al-Kitab is not something that we can be so certain about.

And then thirdly, the gray area comes about the mechanism of slaughter itself, and this third issue can be divided into two subcategories. 3A: the issue of stunning, or electrocution, or the bolt gun. All of these things bring about an uncertainty: is the animal alive at the time of slaughter or not? If the animal is dead by the stunning, then it doesn't matter if you slaughter or not; it will be considered dead meat. It is not slaughtering. So 3A is about the issue of stunning. It is a gray area; we'll talk a little bit about that. And then 3B is not only the issue of stunning, but the issue of how the knife is used on the neck of the animal. Because these days there is a rising trend of what is called the vertical cut rather than the horizontal cut, and this vertical cut is highly problematic from an Islamic standpoint because it does not slice the jugular veins. As we'll come to, that is yet another issue.

So this is, in a nutshell, the position that I defend, which is the majority position: that it is not allowed to eat non-zabihah meat, and that when Allah has allowed the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab, He has allowed it if they follow their own conditions and their own Shari'ah. And therefore that ayah, the verse in the Qur'an that the meat of the People of the Book is allowed for you, applies to what we now call in our times kosher meat. **Kosher meat is halal; that is what Allah references in the Book. As for the regular meat available, they have not followed their Shari'ah, so it will not be considered permissible.** That is the short answer.

Now, for those that are interested in the longer answer, please bring out your pen and paper, or start writing, because this is going to be a bit of a more detailed lecture. I decided to go into detail because this is a topic that everybody asks about and everybody is wondering about. And this is still a brief introduction, despite the fact that it is an entire lecture. Obviously fiqh is never-ending; you can go deeper and deeper.

The more detailed issue begins as follows. First and foremost, I want to advise myself and all of you to please remove the emotionalism from this question. All too often both sides become very emotional: the side that eats the meat that is available, and the side that is very strict in their stance on zabihah. And the reason why they get emotional is, I think, self-explanatory. The ones that are eating the meat are being accused of doing haram, and obviously they get on the defensive: "What do you mean? I'm following Shaykh so-and-so." And the ones that are not eating that meat really feel left out when they see their friends go to the burger joints and eat the Chicken McNuggets, or whatever it is, the delicious steaks. And so they really feel like it's not fair: "I'm giving up; why don't they give up?" And so that feeling of "it's not fair," rather than saying, "You know what, Allah will reward me for my sacrifice," they channel that, and they kind of become irritated.

I request both sides to really remove the emotionalism and realize that there are two opinions. Those that choose to do it: you have followed a position that many 'ulama of our times state, as I'm going to mention. And those that choose to abstain: you have followed the more pure position, and there's no doubt, inshallah, that Allah will reward you for your extra piety. So remove the emotionalism.

Now, with that having been said, we begin by setting up the basic principle of the entire discussion. This is a very interesting point that most people don't even think about when they talk about the issue of meat. Meat in the Shari'ah: the default is that if you don't know where it is from, it is haram. This is a principle that most people don't know. Anonymous meat (I should not say anonymous, but ambiguous meat): if somebody puts a platter in front of you and you have no idea where it came from, if you find slaughtered meat somewhere and you don't know the origin, the default is that you assume that it is haram.

Now, this is in contrast to pretty much everything else in the Shari'ah, where the default is that it is halal. I have said this many times about the default when it comes to interaction with human beings, personal interactions, monetary transactions, food and clothing overall.

Now, this is interesting. If we were to discover an exotic animal on some untouched island, and there is no name that's been given to this animal, the default is that the animal is halal overall, unless we find, for example, that it has claws or it's hunting. So there are specific conditions: every predator that has claws, for example. This is one condition: if it is a predator that has claws, it becomes haram. Otherwise, by default, the animal is halal.

Now suppose you went to some exotic resort somewhere and they're presenting meat to you that is slaughtered. They bring it to the table and you don't know where it came from. In this case, the animal itself, the default is that it is halal, but that's obviously theoretically speaking: you have to slaughter it. The meat that is coming to you slaughtered and cooked, the default is that it is haram, unless you know the origin.

So in this case the general rule will be (and this is a famous principle of fiqh; Imam al-Shatibi mentions it in his al-Muwafaqat) that when it comes to the issue of meat, the asl is that it is not allowed until we know that it is slaughtered properly. Imam al-Nawawi, in his Sharh of Sahih Muslim, mentions the hadith and says that in this particular hadith there is a very important principle: if there is a doubt about whether the animal has been slaughtered properly or not, then the default is that we assume that it has not been slaughtered properly. And then he says there is no difference of opinion about this issue.

So we need to begin the entire discussion by saying the onus of proof is on the one who says that meat is halal. Otherwise, the default is that the meat is indeed haram, if we do not know where the meat comes from.

Now, obviously I am not saying that we need to see the actual plate in front of us, from the slaughterhouse to the plate. No, what I'm saying is there needs to be a reasonable assumption. If you go to a Muslim butcher and he is saying that he has slaughtered it in a proper manner, then you trust the Muslim butcher and you may purchase from this shop, and the burden is on the person who is saying he has slaughtered it in a halal manner. So if you go to a restaurant and they're advertising, "We are serving only zabihah meat," and the owners are Muslims and whatnot (or even if they're non-Muslims, but they are trustworthy, that they're not going to lie), you see their certificate. So now there's a level of reasonable certainty that what they are advertising is halal, and that in this country they will be sued, there's going to be a huge lawsuit, if they are lying, and there's no reason for them to do that. So you make a reasonable assumption. If they're advertising it as halal, or if the Muslim is saying he slaughtered it in the slaughterhouse, then inshallah you will take his word for it. You do not have to have seen it slaughtered.

At the same time, if you don't know, and it is completely unknown where the meat is coming from, it's presented in front of you, for example, in this case the default is that you will not consider it to be halal until you find out. And you may ask the owner of the restaurant, "Is this halal? Is this zabihah?" or whatnot.

Now, the question we're going to answer is: what makes the slaughtering halal? And obviously I keep on saying that all the lectures I give and all of the questions I answer, these are not very detailed. They're kind of intermediate, because for more detail than this, you need many, many hours of discussion.

The main hadith in this regard is muttafaq 'alayh, in Bukhari and Muslim. Rafi' ibn Khadij said, "O Messenger of Allah, sometimes I'm in the desert and I don't bring my knife with me, and I come across, let's say, a rabbit. How can I make that animal halal?" So our Prophet ﷺ said (listen to this hadith; it is in Bukhari and Muslim): "Anything that causes the blood to gush out" (anything that causes the blood to flow from the neck) "and you have mentioned the name of Allah, you may eat of that."

This hadith is the basis of the entire chapter of slaughtering. The blood of the jugular vein must flow out. The whole purpose of the slaughter is to minimize the amount of blood that is left in the body, and when you slaughter the animal properly, the blood will gush out automatically. And you must mention the name of Allah. So everything that causes the blood to gush out, and you have mentioned the name of Allah, you may eat of that.

Now, our scholars have extrapolated from this many different rulings, and let us begin with the first of these rulings, which is mentioned in the Qur'an. The first ruling is that the one who slaughters the animal must be a person who believes in Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and from our Shari'ah's perspective, that means three faith traditions: Muslim, Christian or Jew.

The concession of eating the slaughter of the Ahl al-Kitab was revealed very late in the Shari'ah, in one of the last surahs to be revealed, Surah al-Ma'idah verse five. Allah says in the Qur'an that the food of the people who believe in the Book is halal for you. When Allah says "the food," by unanimous consensus what is meant is the slaughter. As for the food meaning the rice and the vegetables and the grain, you don't even have to be Ahl al-Kitab. You can purchase rice from an atheist; you can purchase vegetables from a Buddhist; it doesn't matter. When Allah says "the food of the People of the Book," what He means is the slaughtering of the People of the Book. So Allah is saying the slaughtering of the People of the Book is halal for you. So the slaughtering of a Muslim or a Christian or a Jew: this is something that is permitted in our religion, if all of the conditions are met.

Now, there's a bit of a deeper discussion about what constitutes a Christian. For example, the sect known as Mormonism: would they count or not? This is a discussion beyond the scope of my brief talk over here. But it is very clear that Christians who believe in the Trinity, and Christians who believe in the divinity of Jesus Christ, are considered Christian by the Qur'an itself. There are many average Muslims who come and say, "How can I eat the slaughter of a Kitabi when he believes that Jesus is the son of God, when he believes in a Trinity?" And I respond to them: the Qur'an criticizes the Trinity in Christianity, and the Qur'an criticizes the claim that Jesus Christ is the son of God, and yet the Qur'an also says that the slaughter of the same Kitabi whose theology is criticized (by the way, Kitabi means a Jewish or Christian person), the slaughter of this Kitabi, is permissible. Therefore the believing Christians and the believing Jews: their slaughter is permissible for us.

And for the record, I believe that those Christian sects that believe in prophets after the Prophet 'Isa (and that is not our Prophet), so the group that was founded in America, and they have their own prophet, Joseph Smith, for example: technically they would not constitute Kitabis. This is my personal ijtihad, and Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best. But Protestants and Eastern Orthodox and Russian Orthodox and Greek Orthodox and mainstream Catholics, and all of these ecumenical groups, Unitarians, Universalist Christians: these are the mainstream Christian groups. They believe in the principles of Christianity, and if amongst them they slaughter the animal and they follow the rules that they're supposed to follow, then that animal would be permissible for us.

Now, why is the slaughter of a non-Kitabi not allowed? If we were to go to a person who's a Buddhist, a person who's a Hindu, and they were to slaughter an animal, why would that slaughter not be allowed? That is very simple. Allah says in the Qur'an, with regards to the People of the Book: "Your God and our God is the same God." They might have a different conception of that God; they might have a different understanding, of the Trinity, obviously, and Jesus Christ. But at the end of the day, they believe in the God of Abraham; they believe in the God of the Children of Israel; they believe in the God of Isaac. So it is the same God. This is in the Qur'an: "Your God and our God is the same God, and we have submitted to Him." In contrast to this, a Buddhist or an atheist obviously does not believe in a God; or a Hindu: their gods are different than ours. So if they were to slaughter an animal, then it is not considered acceptable, because they are not sacrificing to the correct, if you like, deity, the only true deity.

And this plays a very important role when we come to... So this is the first issue, and that is the religion of the one slaughtering. In order for the slaughter to be permissible, the person must be a believing Muslim, a believing Christian or a believing Jew.

Now, of course, in the modern cultures that we live in... Had we lived in America 100 years ago, we would say this condition is no problem. Given that the rates of agnosticism and atheism, especially in Europe, have skyrocketed, this becomes a very ambiguous question in and of itself. Can we make such a presumption, that the societies we live in are believing Christians and Jews? And by the way, there was a poll done by a European company across Europe. A question was asked: "Do you believe in the existence of God?" Not even Christian; just, "Do you believe in God?" Only 51% across Europe said yes. 49% had other answers: spirituality, or some higher power, not God. And the 51%, by the way, wasn't even Christian; it was just generically, "Do you believe in a God or not?" And so around half the people in Europe now would not be able to answer the question, "Do you believe in God?" How can an assumption be made that this is a Kitabi society?

Now, in America, granted, the statistics are relatively higher. I think last I checked it was around 70% or so. But still, 70% is good, but it's not like 90 or 95%. So this whole issue of whether we can assume the society around us is a Kitabi society or not: it's a gray area, and that's one area that needs to be brought in.

And by the way, me personally, my position here: by and large, in the slaughterhouses down south, in Texas where we are, and in Alabama, in places that are basically down south in America, I think it is a very reasonable assumption to make that the bulk of the population are Christians and they believe in God. I don't think that is unreasonable. Now, that's down south. Up north in America, or in Canada, or in Europe, me personally, I think this is a very, very difficult extrapolation to make, and that should give people pause right then and there. That's the first condition: Jewish, Christian or Muslim. And by the way, we can make a presumption: if 95% of the people are Christian, you can make a presumption that the person slaughtering is going to be a Christian.

The second condition: how does the slaughtering occur? That is because, obviously, even if a Jewish or Christian or Muslim person comes and he takes a stick and beats the animal to death, obviously that's not going to be permissible, is it? So it's not just the religion of the one slaughtering; there is how the slaughtering occurs.

How the slaughtering occurs is, again, a very long discussion. Very quickly: the slaughtering must be done via a sharp instrument that slaughters at the throat level and cuts the appropriate passages in the neck of the animal while the animal is alive. If the animal is dead, it doesn't matter if you cut its neck; it is a dead animal. If, a'udhu billah, you run over an animal, or you beat an animal to death, or you electrocute it to death, or you use a stun gun and the animal dies, and then the knife comes to the neck, it doesn't matter even if a Muslim says Bismillah a million times. If the animal is dead, it is dead. It is called in Arabic maytah, or carrion, an animal that is explicitly haram by the testimony of the Qur'an. So the animal must be alive, and a sharp instrument must be used that cuts off...

Now, there are four primary passages in the neck of the animal. You have the trachea, which is the air passage; you have the esophagus, which is the food passage; and then you have the two jugular veins. These are the four main passages in the neck of the animal. There's a lot of discussion amongst the four madhhabs, and more than the four madhhabs, about what if you cut less than the four. By unanimous consensus, the ideal cut is all four: you cut the trachea and the esophagus and both jugular veins. And by the way, in animals they are within an inch or two, an inch and a half, so basically, if you just cut deep enough, you've done all four.

Now, there's a bit of a controversy: what if you do two of the four, three of the four? Inshallah, generally speaking, in the position that I follow, as long as you cut at least one of the jugular veins, then you are fine. Because the purpose is literally as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Everything that causes the blood to flow." That needs to be done, and the blood will only flow if you have cut the jugular vein. If you only cut the esophagus, for example, that's not really going to cause the blood to flow.

And this leads us to another major problem that we have, especially in Western societies, and those problems are twofold: number one, the issue of stunning, and number two, the issue of the cut.

As for the issue of stunning: Western law believes that if you stun the animal, that is more humane. This is their version of humanity. In our version, in the Shari'ah, the stunning is a bigger torture than the killing of the animal itself. If you slaughter the animal with one sharp blade, and you slaughter it the way that the Shari'ah requires it to be slaughtered, then the pain is negligible, if there even is pain. As for electrocution and stun guns and bolt guns and carbon monoxide poisoning, whatever: this is more of a torture from our perspective. But there's nothing we can do. The laws of the land mandate (as far as I know, almost all states mandate) that there must be a type of stunning done.

Now, stunning in and of itself is makruh. It is discouraged. Why is it discouraged? Because from our perspective it tortures the animal. But the stunning will not make the animal haram. What will make the animal haram? If the stunned animal dies before the slaughtering occurs, then that animal is considered maytah, or carrion.

Now, generally speaking, chickens that are slaughtered by machine slaughter are dipped in water that has an electric voltage (I forgot the amps there), but it is something that will stun the chicken. Generally speaking, by and large, it's not going to cause the chickens to die.

However, cows are a totally different issue. That is because in order to stun a cow there are two methods that are used, and the most common one is the stun gun. You take a gun that has a piston, and it's going to be shot out of the cylinder of the gun; it will enter into the forehead of the animal, and then it's going to be brought back out. If you watch videos of this, it is pure torture, and I cannot believe why people think that this is more humane than the Islamic or the kosher method of simply slaughtering the animal. But that is what they believe. When you do that, the animal is absolutely stunned. It is shivering; it is barely able to stand up; it collapses. It's a very sad reality, and we wish that we could change this law, but we cannot do anything in this regard right now.

And so in this process, by the time the animal is then mounted up and the cutting is done, a percentage of those animals die. If the animal is alive, the heart is beating, by the time the blade cuts across the neck, then it is halal, even if it was impermissible... it is makruh. So let's not confuse between the two. To stun the animal, to shoot that gun: this is a type of torture, and we don't like doing this. But if the animal is alive, and the slaughter occurs after the stunning and the animal is alive, the meat will be halal. It is zabihah.

The problem comes if the stunning kills the animal. Studies have been done; a number of studies I have read, and I've spoken to many people that are involved in the business. There is no one number that is universal. I've heard figures from 10 to 20 to 30 to 40 about what percentage of cows don't make it before the slaughtering occurs. And this is not a trivial matter. If 20% or 30% of animals are dead by the time the slaughtering occurs, then, a'udhu billah, that is maytah, that is a dead animal. It doesn't matter: even if a Muslim says Bismillah and slaughters it, it will be haram to eat. So this is yet another factor.

And yet another factor when it comes to how the animal is slaughtered is that these days there is another cut. It is not common, but it is being done by some of the more famous companies or brands, and they call this the vertical cut rather than the horizontal cut. Generally speaking, when you slaughter the animal there should be a horizontal cut. What is happening now in some abattoirs is that they hang the animal upside down (the cow, obviously) and they slaughter it with the vertical cut. And they have their philosophy, which is that they want to keep the blood inside the animal. So they vertically cut the animal, and they cut off just the trachea, the air passage. They just want the animal to die because it cannot breathe, and the blood is left inside. And this cut, according to the majority of our 'ulama, and obviously common sense, will not be considered having slaughtered the animal, because our Prophet ﷺ said, "Everything that causes the blood to gush out," and when you cut the trachea, you are not causing the blood to gush out.

Why would they want to keep the blood inside the animal? Two reasons, they tell us. Number one, because the blood makes the butcher house messy, and they want to keep it cleaner. And number two, according to them, they like the taste (a'udhu billah, and from our perspective we find it disgusting); they like the taste of the meat when there's extra blood in it. Whereas for us, we want to get rid of the blood as much as possible. We want the meat to have as little of the flowing blood as possible; in fact, we want the blood to flow out as much as possible.

So this is another gray area that comes in, about how the animal is slaughtered, and there's no doubt that further research needs to be done. The questions are as follows. Number one: what percentage of cows, and even chickens, are alive by the time the knife comes across the throat? For chickens, generally speaking, enough studies have been done that we're fairly confident to state that the stunning does not kill too many chickens; it's a very negligible amount. And the Shari'ah is not asking for 100%, but it should be the presumption, the prevalent assumption, that we can derive. And number two: which slaughterhouses use the vertical cut versus the horizontal cut? Any slaughterhouse that uses the vertical cut, for sure, is one that we should avoid. But until we find out, another gray area comes in. So we're now at point number two, and that is the slaughtering procedure. Points number one and two together are gray areas; you're compounding them.

Point number three is without a doubt the clear-cut area, which is why I personally follow the majority position, which states that it is not allowed to eat the meat that is available in the marketplace. And what is point number three? Point number three is the issue of saying the name of Allah at the time of slaughter. In Arabic it is called tasmiyah, to say "Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim." And this is really the crux of the matter. It's an open-and-shut case, in that if you believe that saying the name of Allah is a necessary requirement, then obviously the meat available in these countries becomes haram, because we know for a fact that no religious ceremony is done for the average meat available. No God is mentioned; no religious symbolism takes place. It is a completely agnostic, secular institution, and there is no mentioning of the name of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And if you follow the position that saying the name of Allah is not obligatory (which, as we'll come to, is the position of some of the scholars), then in this case you still have the first two issues to worry about: is the person a Christian or Jew, and has the slaughter been done? And those are both gray areas.

So let us discuss the issue of saying Bismillah. The majority of 'ulama, and three of the four madhhabs, state that, ideally speaking, it is an obligation to say Bismillah at the time of slaughter. Now, why do I say ideally? Because if a person forgets, and they had it in their mind... If you get nervous, right? You're going to slaughter the cow, and the cow is moving too much, and you forget to say Bismillah, but you had it in your mind. That's why I'm saying ideally. So we're not talking about the one who forgets even though he wanted to say it; we're talking about the one who had no desire to say Bismillah, the one who had no intention to say Bismillah, or "in the name of Allah."

And by the way, when I say to say Bismillah, it doesn't have to be in Arabic. Somebody is going to say, "Do you really think a Jewish or a Christian person will say Bismillah?" I will respond: they can say "in the name of God," or they can say in Hebrew "in the name of the Lord," which is what the Jews say. No problem. They have to mention the name of their God, of our God; it is the same God. And they have to make the animal holy. What gives us the right to kill an animal? Allah gave us that right. We have no right to kill another animal without mentioning the name of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Allah has given us that right, and therefore the animal will only be permitted if we mention the name of Allah before we sacrifice that animal.

So the position of the Hanbali school and the Maliki school and the Hanafi school, three of the four schools, the position of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim, the position of the majority and the bulk of the Ummah, is that it is a necessary requirement to say the name of Allah before you sacrifice an animal. And any person who intentionally, knowingly, does not say the name of Allah, that animal will be considered haram to eat: maytah, non-halal, non-zabihah. This is the position of three of the four madhhabs.

What is left? One school of law, and that is the Shafi'i school of law. The Shafi'i school was the only school that said mentioning the name of Allah is encouraged but not wajib. It is sunnah, but not wajib. And if you don't mention the name of Allah, even intentionally, then no big deal; the animal is still permitted. So this is the main difference between the two schools when it comes to the issue of saying Bismillah.

Now, what is the evidence of the first school, that you have to say "Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim"? There are numerous evidences in the Qur'an and in the Sunnah. For example, Surah al-Hajj verse 34: Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says, "We have given sacrificial rites to every single nation so that they may mention the name of Allah over the animals that Allah has given them." Also in Surah al-Hajj verse 28, Allah 'azza wa jall says, "so that they may mention the name of Allah," once again, "over the animals that Allah has given them." And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala also says in the Qur'an, "Mention the name of Allah as the animals are lined up to be sacrificed." Again, this is very explicit.

And Allah 'azza wa jall says in Surah al-Ma'idah verse four: "They ask you what animals they are allowed to eat. Say: Allah has allowed you to eat the animals that your falcons or your hunting dogs catch. So go ahead and train them, and then send them out, and eat from that over which you have mentioned the name of Allah and which they have caught for you." Now, hunting animals: even with the hunting animal, Allah says, "Mention the name of Allah." And what this means is that when you send your falcon (you know, the Arabs to this day train their falcons to hunt different types of rabbits and whatnot), when you send your falcon out, you must say Bismillah when you send it out. Then it's going to catch the hare or the rabbit, and it will bring it back to you. And Allah is saying: no problem, you have trained this animal, it's going to go hunt for you, but make sure you say the name of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Notice how explicit this is.

And also the famous hadith we just mentioned, of Rafi' ibn Khadij: "Everything that causes the blood to flow, and you have mentioned the name of Allah." And the hadith in Sahih Bukhari as well, that the Prophet was asked about hunting dogs, and he said: if you let loose your hunting dog and you mention the name of Allah when you send it out, and then when you get there you find another animal eating from the hunted animal, and you don't know which of the two killed the animal, do not eat, because you only said Bismillah over your trained animal, and you did not say Bismillah over the other animal.

By the way, this is one of the main principles that shows you that when meat is unknown, the default is that it is haram. I need you to understand this scenario, because it is one of the most explicit scenarios. The scenario is as follows. You are hunting and you see a deer, or a baby deer or something, and you send your animal to catch this prey. The animal is trained (obviously you're allowed to eat from the trained animals), and it catches it, but it's out of your distance. You go there and you find another animal, another dog, let's say, eating from your hunted animal, and you don't know which of the two animals killed your hunted prey. The Prophet ﷺ said: don't eat, because you only said Bismillah for your animal; you did not say Bismillah for the other animal. Ibn Taymiyyah says this is the most explicit evidence that saying Bismillah makes the animal halal and not saying Bismillah makes the animal haram. This is crystal clear, Ibn Taymiyyah says, and I think it is crystal clear to all of us.

And Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani said, "O Messenger of Allah, I come from a place where people hunt with bows and arrows, and they hunt with trained dogs, and they are also training their dogs to hunt. So tell me what is halal for me." So the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whatever you hunt with your bow and you mention the name of Allah, eat. Whatever your trained dog catches and you have mentioned the name of Allah, eat. And if you are still training the dog, it's not fully trained, then only eat if you're able to catch it when it is still alive." So these are three explicit cases, and the first two are explicit: only if you have mentioned the name of Allah. As for the third, when the dog is still being trained, you cannot eat unless you find it still alive; then you slaughter it and you mention the name of Allah. Because when it's still being trained, you don't know; the dog might be catching it for itself, in which case the animal would not be allowed to eat. The trained animal, by the way, the trained falcon, the trained hunting dog, does not hunt for itself; it hunts for you. If it's hunting for you, you may eat of the meat, but if it's hunting for itself, then you cannot eat of the meat. So this is the reason why.

Also in the Qur'an, Surah al-An'am verses 120 and 121 are very explicit. Surah al-An'am verses 120 and 121: Allah says, "Go ahead and eat of that over which Allah's name has been mentioned, if you believe in Him. And what is the matter with you that you do not want to eat of that over which Allah's name has been mentioned, and it has been made clear to you what has been made haram for you, unless you are forced to do so?" So Allah is basically saying: why are you hesitant to eat the meat? And this is because there were certain animals that in Jahiliyyah, in pre-Islam, were earmarked superstitiously as being haram. So, don't quote me on this, but let's say the third female born to the third female: if you had three female camels and then the third one has three female camels, maybe the third of the third. They had their bad-luck numbers, basically; they had their issues that are just complete mythology. So Allah is saying: go ahead and eat of all of this; destroy that paganism. If you mention the name of Allah, go ahead and eat. Then Allah is saying: why would you not eat when Allah's name has been mentioned?

And then this is the most explicit verse in the whole Qur'an about this issue. Please make a note of it, write it down, go read it yourself: Surah al-An'am verse 121. "Do not eat of the meat over which Allah's name has not been mentioned, for indeed that is a sin." To eat the meat of an animal over which Allah's name has not been mentioned: that is a sin. So this is something that is very, very clear.

And Ibn Taymiyyah, for the advanced students here: I want you to know that he wrote an entire treatise (and you won't find it in Majmu' al-Fatawa, because it is in the recently discovered manuscripts). This is in Jami' al-Masa'il, edited by Dr. Bakr Abu Zayd, volume six, page 377 onwards. He wrote an entire treatise, an entire booklet, about the issue of saying Bismillah. It's a very amazing booklet. And in it he states, and I quote, that the obligation of saying Bismillah before the hunting or before the slaughtering of the animal is more clear from the Qur'an and Sunnah than the obligation of reciting Surah al-Fatihah during the salah. There are more verses and more ahadith about saying Bismillah before you slaughter than about reciting al-Fatihah in the salah. This is what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah writes.

Okay, so this is the position of the Hanafis and Malikis and the Hanbalis: that you must mention the name of Allah, and that if a person intentionally does not (meaning he has no desire to mention the name of Allah), then even if they slaughter it properly, the animal will be considered not allowed.

Jayyid. The Shafi'is are the one school that said that it is not something that is obligatory. And they interpret the verse in the Qur'an, "Do not eat the meat over which Allah's name has not been mentioned," as an animal that dies naturally. Or some of them say this is the meat that has been sacrificed to the gods. And we respond to them: okay, I mean, that's an interpretation, but the verse doesn't say that. The verse is very, very broad and vague: "Do not eat the meat over which Allah's name has not been mentioned." This includes dead animals; this includes sacrificing to other than Allah; and this also includes that over which nothing has been mentioned, which is the default in the lands that we live in.

And the Shafi'is also use a hadith which is in the Sunan of al-Daraqutni, one of the tertiary books of hadith. It's not one of the famous six or seven or eight or nine books; it is beyond that. In the Sunan of al-Daraqutni there is a hadith that says a Muslim who sacrifices, his sacrifice is using the name of Allah. His sacrifice automatically includes Bismillah; whether he says it or not, it includes Bismillah. So they say that this is something that is incorporated into the act of slaughter by the Muslim.

And they also say there's a hadith in Sahih Bukhari (listen to this, because this is always used) that Aisha said that a group of people came to the Prophet ﷺ and said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, groups of people gift us meat, and we do not know whether they have mentioned the name of Allah over that meat or not." So the Prophet ﷺ said, "You go ahead and say Bismillah, and then eat." And then Aisha says that this group of people whom they were asking about were new converts to Islam, hadithu 'ahd. They were new converts to Islam. And so the question arose: maybe they haven't learned the laws of dhabh. And so they're giving us meat; they have just converted a week ago, two weeks ago, and then they're gifting us meat, and we don't know: are they slaughtering properly or not? So the Prophet ﷺ said: you go ahead and say Bismillah, and then go ahead and eat from it. So the Shafi'is say this shows that the Bismillah is not obligatory.

To respond to both of these hadith, the Daraqutni one and the Bukhari one: as for the Daraqutni one, we say that it is considered weak by every single scholar of hadith, including the Shafi'i scholars. There is a weakness in the chain, and fiqh is not based on weak hadith.

As for the hadith in Bukhari, this is actually an evidence against them and not for them. Why? Because the issue is not about whether we should say Bismillah or not. The issue is: should we trust a Muslim when they slaughter an animal? The hadith was not in the context of the Ahl al-Kitab; it was not in the context of completely anonymous meat. It was in the context of meat that has been slaughtered by fellow Muslims, and the Sahabah were wondering whether it is halal or haram because of whether they said Bismillah or not. In fact, this demonstrates (listen to this) that the Sahabah understood that if no Bismillah had been said, the meat would be haram. That's why they're saying, "We don't know whether they said Bismillah or not." If the Bismillah were not obligatory, the Prophet should have said, "Who cares? What difference does it make to you?" But it is obligatory, and so he said, essentially: they're your fellow Muslims; don't doubt them.

Remember, this is for fellow Muslims, and the question was: have they studied the laws of the Shari'ah yet? Do they know how to slaughter yet or not? And the Prophet said: don't open this. Don't go spying on new Muslims; don't quiz and interrogate; assume the best of your fellow Muslims. When you walk into a butcher shop that's owned by a Muslim, don't ask too many questions. As long as you can see this is a righteous person, you understand this person, then Bismillah, go for it. So this hadith is not about tasmiyah, but rather the issue of not being suspicious of other Muslims, and that we should not be hunting for their faults.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, the famous Maliki scholar, says: in this hadith it is understood that the meat slaughtered by a Muslim should be consumed on the assumption that the tasmiyah has been mentioned, because with regards to a Muslim, one should entertain nothing but good thoughts, unless concrete evidence is established to the contrary. This is the famous Ibn 'Abd al-Barr. And Ibn Hajar, who is a Shafi'i scholar himself, commented on this hadith and said: this hadith shows that we should have husn al-zann of other Muslims; think the best thoughts of other Muslims.

So this hadith has nothing to do with it. A lot of Muslims say, "Oh, the Prophet said, you say Bismillah, you'll be fine." No, read the whole hadith. He never said this when it came to meat that you know for a fact no Bismillah was said over. He said it over meat that comes from a Muslim, and that meat, you don't know whether they followed the Shari'ah or not. The Prophet said: assume they did, and if you're in doubt, you say Bismillah. So the hadith cannot apply to the situation where we know for a fact that no Bismillah was said.

Now, all of this we have talked about is applicable to a Muslim slaughtering. Is there any difference when a Kitabi slaughters, when a Christian or Jew slaughters? Is there any difference here?

So the Hanafis said there is absolutely no difference whatsoever. The famous Hanafi mufassir and faqih al-Jassas says: can't you see, or don't you realize, that it is only allowed to eat of the Kitabi's meat if he mentions the name of Allah, and if the Kitabi does not mention the name of Allah, then his zabihah is not halal. This is explicit in the Hanafi madhhab. The other great scholar, Badr al-Din al-'Ayni, who wrote a commentary on Sahih Bukhari, said that if the Kitabi leaves the tasmiyah on purpose, or he mentions the name of other than Allah, then by unanimous consensus it is not allowed to eat that meat. (He is saying unanimous consensus, but it is not a unanimous consensus; or maybe he meant unanimous in his madhhab; otherwise it is not unanimous.) So the Hanafis are very clear.

The Hanbalis as well are very clear. In Ahkam Ahl al-Dhimmah of Ibn al-Qayyim, we find the report that Abu 'Abdullah, meaning Imam Ahmad, was asked about eating the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab, and he said (listen to this, Imam Ahmad is saying): there is no problem with the sacrifice of the Kitabi as long as he sacrifices for Allah and in the name of Allah. So he must sacrifice for Allah and in the name of Allah. And Ibn Qudamah, perhaps the greatest scholar of the Hanbali madhhab of the seventh century, Ibn Qudamah who wrote al-Mughni, says in volume 13, page 311 (listen to this carefully): if the Kitabi does not mention Allah's name on purpose, then the meat is not permissible. It's very clear. If the Kitabi does not mention it, and he's quiet, then that meat will not be permissible.

So the Hanafis and the Hanbalis are very clear. By the way, I should mention that with the Hanbalis, as usual (as any Hanbali student knows), there are always two or three riwayat, and so there are other positions, not the mu'tamad or the famous ones, that do allow. But the one that is the mainstream position of the Hanbali madhhab says that the Kitabi must also mention the name of Allah.

As for the Shafi'is: because they said that the tasmiyah is not necessary for the Muslim, then obviously they also said that the tasmiyah is not obligatory for the Kitabi. So that's fine. So the Hanafis, the Hanbalis and the Shafi'is are all saying the same applies.

Interestingly, the Malikis are the only school that made a distinction between the Muslim and the Kitabi. The Malikis said that saying Bismillah is obligatory for the Muslim but not obligatory for the Kitabi. So they had this distinction over here. In al-Sharh al-Saghir of al-Dardir (which is basically their main matn, or one of the main textbooks of the Malikis), he mentions: it is obligatory for the Muslim to mention the name of Allah in any manner, whether they say SubhanAllah or Allahu Akbar or La ilaha illallah or Bismillah. They just have to say something, for the Muslim. As for the Kitabi, all that we require of the Kitabi is that they don't mention other than Allah; even if they're quiet, their zabihah is permitted. And so the Malikis distinguished, and they said that to say Bismillah is obligatory for the Muslim, not obligatory for the Kitabi. So they made a laxity for the Kitabi, and it is as if they were not as strict with the Kitabi as they were with the Muslim.

Now, the issue comes over here that some people say (and this is something that is found in some of the earlier books; it's not something new): "Look, Allah allowed us to eat their meat, and Allah knew how they would sacrifice. Why are you adding conditions when Allah did not add any conditions?" So this is something that is mentioned in some books of Maliki and Shafi'i fiqh when it comes to the Kitabi. And it is there; nonetheless, it is not a very strong basis for rejecting all of the Qur'an and hadith that explicitly put Bismillah. And I'll tell you why.

Here we apparently have a clash of two sets of evidences. On the one hand, you have an entire long list of ayat and hadith that mention the obligatory nature of saying Bismillah. On the other hand, you have an ambiguous verse that says the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab, or the slaughter of the Ahl al-Kitab, is permitted. Okay: can we form a position that keeps all of these evidences legit? Or should we use one evidence to basically cancel out (not abrogate, but cancel out) the entire other set of evidences? And the response is pretty self-evident. The best thing to do, if you study usul al-fiqh, is to take all of these evidences and apply them equally.

And I'll give you a simple example that everybody will understand. Allah says the slaughter of the People of the Book is permitted for you. Question: when the Christian slaughters the pig, does that become halal or not? Everybody is going to say, of course it doesn't. Excellent. Why? Because Allah has forbidden the pig in other verses. Excellent. So we say Allah has also forbidden eating the meat over which Bismillah has not been said, just like you yourself took the evidence that is very clear. We can say, "Didn't Allah know the Christians are going to eat pigs?" You say, "Of course He knew, but He forbade pig for us." We say the same thing: "Didn't Allah know how they're going to slaughter?" Of course He knows. The knowledge of Allah is not a fiqh argument; it's the evidences. And the evidences say that the meat of the Kitabi is permitted if they follow the law that Allah gave to them and to us.

If the Kitabi beats an animal to death and he eats it, are you going to eat it? You could say, "Allah says, eat it." You will say, "No, no, but it has to be slaughtered." Where did you get that from? Where did you get that it must be slaughtered, when Allah says, "The food of the Ahl al-Kitab is halal for you"? Why did you put the condition that it must be slaughtered? Why did you put the condition that we're not going to eat the pork? Because you found other evidences to limit the scope of application of the verse that says the food of the Ahl al-Kitab is permitted for you.

So we say, similarly, there's one more limitation. Just like we're going to eliminate pork, we're going to eliminate haram animals. If they eat alligators, in our Shari'ah it's not allowed. If they eat other animals of this filthy nature, in our Shari'ah it's not allowed. Let them eat it. Allah is not allowing us to eat just because they're eating. Allah is saying: because they believe in the same God as we do, if they follow the laws and they mention the name of God (unlike a Buddhist or a Hindu)...

Because here's another point: why is it allowed to eat the meat of a Kitabi and not a Buddhist? This goes back to the very beginning of my lecture: because we believe in the same God. If you remove the Bismillah, why can't we eat the meat of a Buddhist? What's the difference there? If he slaughters the animal properly, why can't we? The difference is that the Kitabi and we believe in the same God. So when they mention the name of Allah, that meat will be considered to be slaughtered properly.

And therefore we say that the position of allowing the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab is very explicit, and we affirm this, but only if they follow all of the rulings. And that means the animal must be alive, it must be halal for us, the slaughter must be done with a sharp object, it has to cut one of the jugular veins, and they have to mention the name of Allah.

Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, one of the most famous scholars of the Tabi'un, commented on this verse about the food of the People of the Book being allowed, and he said: that is because they are a religion that believes in a divine book, and they mention the name of Allah. This is Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri. Ibn Kathir says: the ruling that the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book are permissible is agreed upon by the scholars, because the People of the Book believe that slaughtering for other than Allah is prohibited, and they mention Allah's name upon slaughtering their animals, even if they have deviant beliefs about God that do not befit His majesty; but they mention the name of Allah. This is Ibn Kathir. So it's very explicit in our Shari'ah that the point of allowing the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab is that we share the same God. So when the name of Allah is mentioned, then that animal will be halal to eat.

And therefore, dear brothers and sisters, when Allah says the food of the Ahl al-Kitab is halal, this is, for example, kosher meat. It is a mistake of the highest magnitude, in my opinion, to equate kosher with the meat that is available outside in any shop over here: kosher and any meat. If you go to a pious Christian who believes in God, and he wants to give you meat, you say, "Listen, before you slaughter, can you just say 'in the name of God'?" If a pious Christian were to say "in the name of God," I would eat that meat, if it is done properly. If a Christian goes hunting (he's your neighbor, he wants to gift you), you say, "You know what? In our religion, you have to say the name of God. If you don't mind, can you just say the name of God?" If he says, "In the name of God; I said it for you, because I know you want it," that would be permitted. This is when the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab is halal for us.

Now, you're going to say: is that what they do? And the response is: that is definitely what Jewish law, called halakha, requires. Halakha is Shari'ah; halakha is their Shari'ah. In halakhic law, their Shari'ah is actually stricter than our Shari'ah. When they slaughter an animal, can you believe it, they must have a rabbi (like a shaykh and 'alim) present, witnessing everything visually. They have to see that the butcher is slaughtering with only one stroke. The knife has to be a certain number of inches; the knife has to be sharpened a certain number of times; it cannot be done twice. So many different rulings that are stricter than our Shari'ah. And one of the things that they must do is recite this formula in Hebrew, which translates as: "Blessed are You, Adonai our God, Lord of the worlds, who sanctified us through His commandments and instructed us concerning proper animal slaughter. Blessed are You, our Lord." This is the tasmiyah.

Kosher meat: I buy it, and I consider kosher meat to be... By the way, kosher meat; as for kosher products, we're not talking about that, because kosher is broader than meat. I'm talking about kosher meat right now. Kosher products: they have kosher wine. We're not talking about kosher products; we're talking about kosher meat here. Kosher meat is the meat that Allah explicitly allows in Surah al-Ma'idah verse 5.

Now, if for political reasons you want to boycott kosher meat, because of the politics, fully understandable; I'm not saying anything there. But don't bring fiqh into it. The Shari'ah allows the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab, if they slaughter the animal properly and they mention the name of Allah.

Now, you're going to say: how about Christians? Do they mention the name of God? There is no doubt that in our times the bulk of Christianity does not mention the name of God. However, I have been doing some research in this regard, and there are manuals of Christian doctrine and faith, and manuals of Christian living from the past, and some of them explicitly mention this issue. So for example, in the Syriac language of ancient Christianity, there was a great scholar, one of their great priests, by the name of Bar Hebraeus, who died 1286, and he wrote the Nomocanon, or the Book of Laws. And in this he says that the butchers, when they sacrifice the animal, must say, "In the name of Allah, the living God." This is basically Syriac: "in the name of the living God." This is explicit in medieval Christianity, and I'm still doing research here, and I have found other references as well. So it's not that crystal clear that earlier Christians didn't say the name of God. It seems to me that there were many groups of Christians that did mention the name of God in medieval and in early times, and that this is something that especially late Catholic tradition, and of course Protestant...

By the way, Protestant Christianity, which is what we live with: you do understand, if you study your Christianity, Protestant Christianity changed completely the Christian canon, or the Catholic canon. There were actually a number of laws that they had to do. Protestant Christianity says salvation is by faith alone: forget all the law; it's just belief in God; all you've got to do is believe in Jesus Christ. So Protestants are very recent, only 500 years ago, right? Martin Luther came in the 1500s. So understand your Christian history. That's firstly.

Secondly, even if we say that the bulk of Christianity had stopped saying the Bismillah, it doesn't matter, because the bulk of Christianity are eating pork as well. Allah did not allow us to eat pork. Allah said that if the Ahl al-Kitab follow their own Shari'ah (and a part of their Shari'ah is to sacrifice proper animals, to sacrifice with proper utensils, and to mention the name of Allah), then the animal is permitted. And we follow this to this day. If the Christian or Jew does not follow his Shari'ah, and does something haram according to his Shari'ah, how can we make it halal in our own Shari'ah? That's something that is very, very clear.

By the way, Ibn al-Qayyim has a very nice comment about the fact that saying Bismillah makes the animal spiritually pure, and not saying Bismillah makes the animal spiritually impure.

Now, this is in a nutshell; a lot of details we went into. I want to say that, speaking with many scholars of our times, what I've discovered is that it is true that many Shafi'i and Maliki scholars who live in America, or who interact with the Western world, have allowed eating the meat that is available in the marketplaces. And by the way, this is why it needs to be said here: some people think there's a cultural divide, that those from the Indian continent, the desi community, are stricter, and those from the Arab world are more lax. It's not the case. It's that the Shafi'is and the Malikis have a position (the Malikis, by the way, only for the non-Muslim; as for the Muslim, you must say Bismillah). And the Shafi'is and Malikis are the majority among the Arabs, the Egyptians, the North Africans. The North Africans are Maliki; Egyptians and whatnot are generally Shafi'i. So this is why it has become a bit of a cultural issue, even though it should not be a cultural issue.

So some of the Shafi'is and Malikis, maybe even most of them, allow it. However, I have spoken to many of my own personal friends who are Shafi'is and Malikis, and believe it or not, many of them do not eat that meat. Why? Not because of the tasmiyah, but because of the issue of Jew and Christian, because agnosticism is on the rise, and also because of the issue of stunning. And I have many good friends that are Malikis. In fact, I was speaking to one this morning and told him about this, and he told me, "You know what? The fatwa in our books is that technically it's allowed, but that's theoretically. Realistically, we don't even know if the people are Christian or not. We can't make this assumption." So one of my own Maliki friends does not eat the meat because, even though he says, "I agree with the Maliki madhhab in its view that Bismillah is not obligatory for the Kitabi," we don't know whether it's a Kitabi or not. It could be an agnostic, could be a Buddhist, could be anything else, could be an atheist. And also because of the whole issue of how the meat is slaughtered.

The modern Hanafi school, especially of course our Deobandi brethren, are very strict in this regard, and that is following the Hanafi school. Mufti Taqi Uthmani has a very good book in English; it's been translated. If anybody's interested, please buy that book. I forgot the title (maybe somebody can post it in the notes on YouTube), but it's on the meat of the Ahl al-Kitab, or the meat of the West. You can buy it online. It is one of the most comprehensive books in English in this regard, and you can read this book and it will give you all of these evidences and more. And so our Hanafi brethren and our Deobandi brethren are very strict, and they do not eat the meat, by and large.

What I find the most interesting is the Hanbali school, or I should say the modern Salafis, to be more explicit, because what happens here is that I find a pure disconnect between their 'ulama and they themselves. Most of our brethren from that trend do eat the meat available here, and they have a "don't ask, don't tell" policy; they think they can eat it. But if you actually look at their teachers (and of course I studied under many of them myself, and I respect and admire all of those great 'ulama), their teachers, the main icons of that madrasah and school, are all upon the position that you should not eat their meat.

Shaykh Salih al-Fawzan, who is one of the greatest scholars of the modern Salafi school, has his master's dissertation on this topic. He wrote his entire dissertation 50 or 40 years ago on this topic (I read it cover to cover, by the way), and in it he staunchly opposes eating the meat that is available in Western lands. The Permanent Committee, Hay'at Kibar al-'Ulama', also have a fatwa in this regard, that the meat that comes from Europe and America to Saudi Arabia should not be eaten, because there are too many things going on. Shaykh Ibn Baz, the Mufti of Saudi Arabia 15 or 20 years ago, wrote a pamphlet in which he says that if it's doubtful whether the Kitabi said Bismillah or not, then the asl, or the default, is that the meat would not be permitted. He said: if it's doubtful, we're not sure, then we assume that he did not say it.

My own teacher, Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin, Allah yarhamuh, has a fatwa that is very clear, and that is that we don't ask what they do, and we assume that they say Bismillah, and so we should eat. So that is his fatwa. However, I actually studied this chapter with Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin when I was in 'Unayzah, in his village: the chapter of eating and drinking and hunting. And after the lesson was over, I went up to him personally, and we said, "Ya Shaykh, the issue of Bismillah: you are saying 'don't ask, don't tell.' I understand that. But we're not asking; we know for a fact that the slaughterhouses in America do not say Bismillah. We know for a fact they are secular, and they have no religion, and they don't mention the name of God." So he said to us (and I didn't read this in a book, I didn't hear this on a cassette; I heard it with my own two ears, and the Shaykh was 10 feet in front of me), he said to us: "If you are certain that they don't say the name of Allah, then that meat is haram for you to eat."

And so this is the standard fatwa from the mashayikh and the 'ulama of the Salafi school, and I find it interesting that most people who follow that school don't follow their own teachers in this regard. And I find that to be something that doesn't make sense to me. They should follow their teachers, and they should stick with what they consider to be correct, because this is definitely the fatwa... Ibn Taymiyyah, by the way, is very strict in this regard. Ibn Taymiyyah wrote an entire treatise, and I encourage all of you who read Arabic to read that.

So now we summarize and come to a conclusion. It's been a long lecture, but inshallah there is a benefit in this. The summary of the issues pertaining to the meat that is commonly available in the Western world:

The first major issue is that the religion of the one who sacrifices is at best ambiguous. Me personally, as I said, I'm comfortable saying that in most southern U.S. states... California? Not California, scrap that. Definitely, I would say, Texas; California, maybe, I'm not saying no; but Texas and Alabama, these are the states I'm much more familiar with. I'm from Texas, born and raised in Texas. I feel comfortable saying, you know what, the bulk are clearly Christian. The same cannot be said of a slaughterhouse, let's say, in Vermont. The same cannot be said of Canada, Vancouver. The same cannot be said of a slaughterhouse in England, in Brussels, in the Nordic countries. I mean, more than 70% of Denmark and Sweden, for example, are claiming to not believe in God. How can you say this is Ahl al-Kitab? How can you say that? Denmark, by the way: so many meat products come from Denmark, and the rates of agnosticism and atheism are skyrocketing. So that's a major issue right then and there.

The second is, of course, the state of the animal as the instrument cuts the throat. What percentage are alive after stunning? What is the stunning method that is used? What is the slaughtering method that is used? Again, a lot of ambiguity here. And that's why I do have some Maliki and Shafi'i friends who believe that the tasmiyah is not obligatory, but they still don't eat because of these first two issues.

Then the third issue comes, and that is the issue of tasmiyah. And of course this is where we say that the Hanbali school and the Hanafi school are very clear that even the Kitabi must say Bismillah. As for the Malikis, they said the Muslim must and the Kitabi does not have to. And the Shafi'is are consistent: neither the Muslim nor the Kitabi needs to say Bismillah. The position I follow is that of Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim, and it is very clear: the evidences for saying Bismillah being obligatory are more numerous and more clear than the evidences for reciting al-Fatihah in the salah. This is quoting Ibn Taymiyyah.
